01 Antidepressants · class card

SSRIs

selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors · citalopram · escitalopram · fluoxetine · fluvoxamine · paroxetine · sertraline

Practice
  1. 61-year-old man, 3 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction low mood, anhedonia and poor sleep for a month; wants a medicine takes aspirin, metoprolol and a statin electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm, corrected QT at the upper limit of normal → Citalopram → its dose-dependent QT prolongation makes it the SSRI to avoid after a recent myocardial infarction; sertraline and escitalopram are the first choices, with few drug interactions
  2. 46-year-old woman takes tamoxifen after surgery for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer two months of low mood, poor sleep and guilt meets criteria for major depressive disorder; an SSRI is planned no other medicines → Paroxetine → a strong inhibitor of cytochrome P450 2D6, it lowers the active metabolite of tamoxifen; citalopram inhibits that enzyme only weakly, and escitalopram has few drug interactions
  3. 34-year-old woman started sertraline for major depressive disorder 2 weeks ago on a full dose since; sleep a little better, mood unchanged mild nausea in the first days, now gone no suicidal thoughts → Continue sertraline at the same dose → response usually starts at 2 to 3 weeks and can take up to 8; an SSRI gets 6 weeks at full dose before any change, and an abrupt stop can bring discontinuation symptoms
